steps.instruction: A cloud of points has been generated for you. BEFORE dragging anything, predict by eye: roughly where should the best-fit line go? Mentally draw one.
steps.observe: Where do you expect the line's slope and intercept to land?
steps.reveal: Most people are surprisingly bad at this - eyes tend to FLATTEN the slope (a regression-toward-the-mean illusion). The math says the best line balances residuals; the eye often weighs the extremes too heavily.

steps.instruction: Drag the line to your best guess. Watch the squared-error meter as you adjust. Try to minimize it.
steps.observe: Does the meter go down monotonically as you approach what looks like the best line?
steps.reveal: Sum of squared errors (SSE) is the standard objective for OLS - minimize SSE and you get the least-squares line. SSE penalizes big residuals quadratically, so outliers can pull your line away from the bulk.

steps.instruction: Now switch the metric to absolute errors (SAE). Re-fit to minimize that instead. Compare the two best-fit lines.
steps.observe: Are the two lines noticeably different? Where do they disagree most?
steps.reveal: Least-absolute-deviations (LAD) lines weigh each residual equally - they are more robust to outliers. OLS follows squared error and gets dragged toward big residuals; LAD does not. The two agree closely on clean data and diverge when outliers are present.

steps.instruction: Click 'Show OLS best fit' to overlay the mathematical optimum. How close is your by-eye fit to the OLS line?
steps.observe: Was your by-eye intercept too high or too low? Slope too steep or too flat?
steps.reveal: Most beginners get within roughly plus-or-minus 10-20% of OLS on slope and intercept. The fact that the math gets it 'exactly right' isn't because it is smarter - it is because it minimizes a specific loss (SSE) that you cannot optimize by inspection. The line you find depends on the loss you minimize.

steps.instruction: Reset to a new random seed (or change sigma) to see a noisier dataset. Re-fit by eye. Notice how confidently you can place the line when noise is large vs. small.
steps.observe: How does the UNCERTAINTY of your fit grow with noise?
steps.reveal: Larger sigma (residual SD) makes the by-eye fit more ambiguous - multiple lines look roughly equally good. The standard error of the slope formalizes this: SE(b_1) grows with the residual SD and shrinks with the spread of x. Inference for slope quantifies the uncertainty you just FELT.
